turn.speech: The error means no RLS policy on storage.objects allowed the write. Besides a missing or too-narrow INSERT policy, upsert true also needs SELECT and UPDATE. Does your upload set upsert true, and what SELECT policies exist for that bucket?
turn.text:
The error means Postgres rejected a write to `storage.objects` because no RLS policy allowed it. Storage keeps object metadata in `storage.objects`, and RLS on that table decides who may upload. [1] Without matching policies, Storage allows no uploads. [1]

## Common causes, most likely first

| # | Cause | Why it fails | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No `INSERT` policy on `storage.objects` | Uploading needs an `INSERT` policy. [1] | Add an `INSERT` policy with a `WITH CHECK` clause. |
| 2 | `INSERT` policy exists, but the `WITH CHECK` condition is false for this path | Typical mismatches are the wrong `bucket_id`, a folder prefix that doesn't match, or a role the policy doesn't cover (`to authenticated` versus an anon request). [2] | Compare the actual `bucket_id` and `name` with the policy expression. Check which role the request used. |
| 3 | `upsert: true` without a matching `SELECT` (and `UPDATE`) policy | The docs say overwriting needs `SELECT` and `UPDATE` in addition to `INSERT`. [1] The KB article says upsert runs `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` with `RETURNING *`. A missing `SELECT` policy then fails the whole transaction with this 403. [3] | Set `upsert: false` if you don't need overwrites. Otherwise add a `SELECT` policy that mirrors the `INSERT` policy. [3] |
| 4 | Unauthenticated request, or the wrong identity | Policies like `to authenticated` or `auth.jwt()->>'sub'` don't match an anon request. A folder name derived from `auth.uid()` is also wrong if the user isn't signed in. | Confirm the client has a session when it uploads. |

Cause 3 is the one people miss. The error text says "new row", which suggests an `INSERT` problem. Your `INSERT` policy can be correct and the upload can still fail. [3]

## Example policies

This is the documented pattern for per-user folders. It allows `INSERT` for authenticated users into a folder named after their ID:

```sql
create policy "Allow authenticated uploads"
on storage.objects
for insert
to authenticated
with check (
  bucket_id = 'my_bucket_id' and
  (storage.foldername(name))[1] = (select auth.jwt()->>'sub')
);
```

For overwrites, add matching `SELECT` and `UPDATE` policies. The docs' copy/move page shows `select` and `update` policies keyed on `owner_id`. [4]

These are policy changes to `storage.objects`. They don't touch your data. Test them in a non-production project first. To roll one back, run `drop policy "<name>" on storage.objects;`.

## What I haven't verified

I haven't seen your policy, bucket name, upload path or SDK call. The table above lists candidate causes, not a diagnosis. Which one applies depends on evidence I don't have yet.

Sources, all Tier 1 official Supabase docs, fetched 2026-10-21:
- [1] [Storage Access Control: Access policies](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control.md#access-policies)
- [2] [Storage Access Control: Policy examples](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control.md#policy-examples)
- [3] [KB: Storage error 403 "new row violates row-level security policy" on upload](https://supabase.com/kb/troubleshooting/storage-error-403-forbidden-new-row-violates-row-level-security-policy-on-upload.md#storage-error-403-forbidden-new-row-violates-row-level-security-policy-on-upload)
- [4] [Copy Objects: Permissions](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/management/copy-move-objects.md#permissions)

**Question:** Does your upload call set `upsert: true`? If it does, what `SELECT` policies exist on `storage.objects` for that bucket?
